title: Lee-Yang Theory Guided Force Field Refinement Based on Phase Diagrams
authors: Bin Jin, Qijun Ye, Xinzheng Li, Kuang Yu, Shenzhen Xu
abstract: We propose a general framework for automatic force field refinement guided by phase diagrams, grounded in Lee-Yang phase transition theory. The central idea is to directly use the partition function modulus as a phase-diagram-guided optimization target. Evaluating the modulus at points close to the real axis, where the Lee-Yang zeros are mostly associated with the phase transition, is more physically meaningful and avoids the numerical difficulty of explicitly solving for the zeros. This approach requires no system-specific order parameters or response properties for characterizing phase transition points, making it universal across various discontinuous phase transitions and material systems. We validate the method on refining parameters of a Lennard-Jones potential covering both gas-liquid and solid-liquid transitions, and a Cu embedded-atom method potential based on experimental melting curves. The refined force fields reproduce the target phase diagrams with significant improvement across all systems. For Cu, the refinement simultaneously improves predictions of enthalpy and heat capacity, which are observables beyond the optimization target. These results establish Lee-Yang theory as a practical tool for contemporary force field development.
summary: This paper introduces a novel method to automatically refine interatomic potentials by leveraging Lee-Yang theory. It treats phase transitions as singularities in the partition function, using the modulus of this function as a differentiable target during optimization. The technique successfully improves predictions for both simple models and metallic systems by enforcing consistency with known phase diagrams.
main_problem: Developing a general, automated framework for refining interatomic force fields by guiding the optimization process using information derived from known phase diagrams.
main_result: The proposed method successfully refines potentials (L-J and EAM) such that the predicted Lee-Yang zeros accurately map onto target coexistence curves, significantly improving predictions of thermodynamic properties like enthalpy and heat capacity.
method: It uses Lee-Yang theory to treat phase transitions as singularities in the partition function. The refinement minimizes a loss function based on the modulus of the partition function evaluated at points near the predicted Lee-Yang zeros in the complex temperature plane.
model_or_system: The method is applied to classical molecular simulations, specifically refining parameters for Lennard-Jones potentials (gas-liquid and solid-liquid) and Embedded-Atom Method potentials (Cu metal).
key_observables: Partition function modulus ($\vert 	ilde{Z} \vert$), phase transition temperatures ($T_{coex}$), enthalpy $H(T)$, and isobaric heat capacity $C_p(T)$.
important_parameters: The optimization targets are defined by the Lee-Yang circle theorem, requiring input of a known phase diagram boundary.
main_assumptions: The core assumption is that minimizing $\vert 	ilde{Z} \vert$ at points on the Lee-Yang circle correctly guides the force field parameters toward the true thermodynamic equilibrium state.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the theoretical concept of Lee-Yang zeros forming a circle in the complex plane, show optimization results comparing initial vs. refined phase diagrams (L-J), and validate improved predictions for $H(T)$ and $C_p(T)$ against experimental data (Cu).
paper_structure: The paper introduces the framework using Lee-Yang theory to guide force field refinement. It details the mathematical construction of the loss function based on the partition function modulus, validates it on L-J systems for multiple transitions, and extends its applicability to metallic potentials like Cu.
why_interesting: While focused on classical condensed matter, the reliance on complex analysis (Lee-Yang zeros) and differentiable optimization techniques makes this methodology highly relevant for developing machine learning force fields that require rigorous thermodynamic constraints.
